mcqs.question: What problem does a "follow-the-sun" on-call model specifically solve for a globally distributed team?
options: It reduces the total number of engineers needed on the team
It automatically resolves incidents without human intervention
It eliminates the need for a secondary on-call engineer
It hands off on-call responsibility to whichever region is currently in business hours, avoiding overnight pages for a team with real 24/7 coverage
mcqs.explanation: Follow-the-sun rotates primary responsibility to the region currently awake, so no single engineer is routinely paged at 3am for a service with genuine round-the-clock global coverage. It doesn't shrink headcount, remove the need for a secondary, or automate resolution.

mcqs.question: Why does correctly assigning severity (SEV1 vs SEV2 vs SEV3) matter beyond just labeling an incident?
options: Severity determines who gets paged, how urgently, and what communication happens — misjudging it in either direction causes real damage
Severity only affects which dashboard the incident appears on
Severity is purely cosmetic and has no operational effect
Severity only matters for billing purposes
mcqs.explanation: Severity directly drives response mechanics: paging urgency, who's pulled in, and whether customers or executives get notified. Over-declaring wastes people's time and creates alarm; under-declaring delays the right people and communication reaching those affected — it's a functional lever, not a label.

mcqs.question: Why does the Incident Commander role deliberately avoid doing the technical debugging themselves?
options: Because ICs are never technical enough to debug
Because tracking multiple workstreams, severity, and comms at the same time as debugging would compromise both jobs, so splitting them keeps each moving well
Because company policy forbids ICs from touching production systems
Because debugging is always delegated to a separate on-call rotation
mcqs.explanation: The IC role is a coordination role by design: doing deep technical debugging while also tracking parallel workstreams and stakeholder communication would degrade both. It isn't about IC technical ability or a hard policy ban — it's a structural choice to keep coordination and fixing from competing for the same person's attention.

mcqs.question: Why is "blameless" in a postmortem considered a functional mechanism rather than just a cultural nicety?
options: Because it means no incident is ever taken seriously
Because it removes personal consequences for any mistake, no matter how severe
Because it's what makes engineers willing to honestly disclose what actually happened, instead of hiding details out of fear of being blamed
Because it lets the team skip writing a root cause section
mcqs.explanation: Blameless postmortems work because they change what people are willing to admit: if disclosing "I ran the wrong command" leads to blame, people quietly obscure the real sequence of events, and the postmortem loses its accuracy. Blameless doesn't mean incidents aren't taken seriously or that root cause is skipped — it means the analysis targets the system, not the individual.

mcqs.question: Which postmortem action item is more likely to actually prevent the same incident from recurring?
options: "Remind the team to double-check config changes before deploying"
"Schedule a team meeting to discuss the incident"
"Ask the engineer involved to be more careful next time"
"Add an automated pre-deploy validation check that rejects configs missing a required field"
mcqs.explanation: A structural safeguard — an automated check that rejects the bad state — doesn't depend on anyone remembering to be careful, so it survives the next tired engineer at 2am. Reminders, individual carefulness, and discussion meetings are all human-vigilance-dependent and have a well-documented tendency to not actually prevent recurrence.
